deep.reconstruction:
This page contains no derivation. It is a documentary copy, apparently in a hand other than Riemann's own (possibly a later editor's or collector's), of the Paris Académie des Sciences announcements about the Grand prix de mathématiques that Riemann competed for. It is filed in the heat-conduction bundle as folio 22r.

(1) The prize question. It was proposed for 1855, re-set for 1857 and extended to 1861. It asks for the thermal state of an infinite homogeneous solid body such that a system of isothermal curves (surfaces) at a given instant remains isothermal at all later times. Equivalently, the temperature at a point must be expressible as a function of time and of only two further independent variables.

In modern terms: find solutions u(x,t), with x in R^3, of the heat equation u_t = div(K grad u) such that u(x,t) = F(t, p(x), q(x)). In this form the level sets of u at any t lie in the family generated by two time-independent functions p and q. In the one-function case, u = F(t, p(x)), the isotherms are permanent families of surfaces.

The announcement also gives the practicalities: a gold medal worth 3000 francs; submission deadline 1 July 1861; sealed-name envelopes.

(2) Excerpt from the Comptes rendus of 8 July 1861. A memoir arrived on 1 July 1861, was registered as no. 2, and was reserved for the future commission. This is Riemann's 'Commentatio mathematica, qua respondere tentatur quaestioni ab Ill.ma Academia Parisiensi propositae', the so-called Pariser Preisschrift.

(3) Excerpt from the Revue de l'instruction publique, no. 40, 2 January 1862. Two memoirs were received and the prize was not awarded. One competitor 'merely sketched a method whose consequences time did not allow him to develop'; this matches Riemann's terse memoir. The other treated elegantly an already-studied case (permanence due to the form and position of the isotherms). It omitted the case the Academy mainly had in mind: isotherms that are permanent because of the law of their initial temperatures. The question was re-set for 1863, with new memoirs or supplements due by 1 January 1863.

(4) A further announcement of the 1862 Grand prix: summarise, discuss and improve the results on plane quartic curves, with a deadline of 1 October 1862.

The page serves to document the context and fate of Riemann's 1861 heat-conduction prize memoir. That memoir reduces the problem, for an anisotropic body, to the question of when a quadratic differential form sum b_ij dx_i dx_j can be transformed to constant coefficients. It introduces the quantities later called the Riemann curvature tensor.
errors: Copying slip: 'il n'a pas possible' should read 'il n'a pas été possible'.
Copying slip: 'ne lui a pas permis développer' lacks 'de' ('permis de développer').
No mathematical errors, since the page contains no mathematics.

results.what: Record of the Paris Academy prize question on heat conduction (permanent isothermal surfaces) and the 1861/62 jury verdict, documenting Riemann's anonymous memoir no. 2
results.modern_name: Riemann's Pariser Preisschrift (1861); the related mathematics is the curvature tensor / flatness criterion for a quadratic differential form
results.usually_credited_to: Riemann (memoir 1861, published posthumously in Werke 1876); the problem itself goes back to Lamé's isothermal surfaces (1837)

deep.surprise_reason: The page is a copied archival record of prize announcements and the jury report. The history of Riemann's 1861 Paris prize memoir, and its non-award, is well documented in Riemann's Werke and the secondary literature (Weber/Dedekind, Laugwitz, Farwell–Knee).

transcription_corrections: The year in 'Revue de l'instruction publique, 21e année' is written with a superscript and is hard to read. 21e/22e année is plausible for 1862, since the Revue began in 1842.
The image has 'il n'a pas possible' as transcribed, but this is the copyist's omission of 'été'.
Folio number '22' is written at the right margin, near the end of the Comptes rendus paragraph.
